Authors Affiliations * 1 Eye Research Center, Farabi Eye Hospital, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Qazvin square, South Karegar Street, 1336616351, Tehran, Iran. * 2 Eye Research Center, Farabi Eye Hospital, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Qazvin square, South Karegar Street, 1336616351, Tehran, Iran. amindehghani.snj@gmail.com. * 3 Eye Research Center, Farabi Eye Hospital, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Qazvin square, South Karegar Street, 1336616351, Tehran, Iran. masoud_mirghorbani2016@yahoo.com. * PMID: 34709453 * DOI: 10.1007/s00417-021-05459-8 Abstract Background: Recently, endothelial keratoplasty (EK) has been increasingly considered the first intervention in pediatrics with isolated corneal endothelial dysfunction. This systematic review aims to investigate the current evidence about the advantages, disadvantages, technical challenges, and clinical outcomes of EK in the pediatric group. Method: All the English literature relevant to pediatric EK was searched in PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane databases with appropriate keywords. Relevant data were pooled to conduct an individual participant data meta-analysis. Results: Of 1646 articles found initially, 35 articles were finally eligible to be included in our study. A total of 154 eyes of 107 patients underwent Descemet's stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK). Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) was the most reported indication for pediatric DSAEK (108 eyes). Descemet's membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) was performed in 2 eyes of 2 cases, one with PPCD and another one in a patient with Kearns-Sayre syndrome. Owing to some specific anatomical and physiological pediatric characteristics, some modifications in a standard procedure were suggested. The average follow-up period was 23.80 ± 20.18 months (3 months to 8.5 years). Seventy-six eyes who had a mean best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 1.36 ± 0.70 (0.49 to 3) logMAR preoperatively found mean BCVA of 0.51 ± 0.33 (0.04 to 2) logMAR postoperatively. Graft dislocation was the most reported complication (26 eyes). The rate of other complications was low. Endothelial cell loss was reported from 8.3 to 63.7% after pediatric EK with follow-up duration from 3 months to 8.3 years. Conclusion: EK procedures, despite some technical challenges, are feasible surgical techniques with acceptable visual and anatomical outcomes in the management of pediatrics with corneal endothelial dysfunction and minimal stromal involvement. fetched_contents.text: Indications and outcomes of pediatric penetrating keratoplasty: A retrospective observational study Abstract Background: Pediatric corneal transplantation can be indicated in congenital and acquired conditions. Challenges include preoperative evaluation, multiple intraoperative obstacles, and postoperative problems in follow-up and management. This study was aimed at identifying the indications and clinical outcomes of pediatric penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) in Jordan. Methods: This retrospective cohort study was conducted in Amman, Jordan. Using the hospital’s electronic database, all medical records of patients aged < 18 years who underwent PKP between January 2004 and October 2019 were reviewed. Preoperative evaluations included best-corrected distance visual acuity (BCDVA) and anterior and posterior segment examinations. Postoperative complications, BCDVA, and graft survival were examined 1 year postoperatively. Results: A total of 149 cases of pediatric PKP were performed on 141 eyes of 118 patients with an age mean ± standard deviation (SD) of 11.44 ± 4.97 years at the time of surgery. Acquired non-traumatic corneal pathologies accounted for 65.8% of indications for PKP. The most frequent indication was advanced keratoconus (55.7%). Preoperative and 1-year postoperative BCDVAs significantly differed (P < 0.001), with 111 (74.5%) patients showing improved BCDVA, 12 (8.05%) patients showing worsened BCDVA, and 26 (17.45%) patients showing no change in BCDVA. The overall 1-year graft survival rate was 80.54%. Conclusions: This was the largest study in Jordan involving pediatric patients who underwent PKP for various indications, showing a significant improvement in BCDVA, with a high survival rate at 1 year. Future studies with longer follow-up periods could provide stronger evidence for surgical outcomes and graft survival. Further, the option of lamellar keratoplasty in the pediatric age group should be assessed. Key Words: pediatrics, penetrating keratoplasty, congenital, acquired, traumatic injuries, corneal grafting, keratoconus, visual acuities INTRODUCTION Pediatric penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) is defined as full-thickness corneal transplantation in patients younger than 18 years of age. It is rarely performed and has a high rate of graft failure and poor visual outcomes [1]. However, it remains the gold standard treatment modality to improve visual acuity, retain structural integrity, and avoid deprivation amblyopia [2-4]. PKP can be indicated in congenital and acquired conditions, with acquired conditions being traumatic or non-traumatic [5]. The practice of PKP differs between developed and developing countries. For instance, the most common indications for PKP are trauma and infection in developing countries and keratoconus and congenital corneal opacities in developed countries [5-7]. Challenges in pediatric PKP include difficult preoperative evaluation; multiple intraoperative obstacles, such as a small eye size, less scleral rigidity, and positive posterior vitreous pressure; and several challenges in post-operative follow-up and management [1, 8, 9]. Nevertheless, the improved understanding of intraoperative and postoperative complications and technologic advancements have led to an increased rate of successful pediatric PKP and decreased the age at which pediatric PKP can be performed [2]. Data on pediatric PKP in the Middle East are limited. This study was aimed at identifying the indications and clinical outcomes of pediatric PKP in Jordan. METHODS This retrospective cohort study was conducted at the Jordan University Hospital (JUH), a tertiary medical center in Amman, the capital of Jordan, from January 2004 to October 2019. We investigated the indications and clinical outcomes of pediatric PKP at JUH over the 15-year study period. The institutional review board of the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Jordan approved the study protocol (approval number 16/204). The requirement for obtaining informed consent was waived owing to the retrospective nature of the study. Using the hospital’s electronic database, the medical records of all pediatric patients who underwent PKP between January 2004 and October 2019 were retrieved. Inclusion criteria were age < 18 years and a minimum follow-up after PKP of 1 year. Five examiners preoperatively examined the patients. Best-corrected distance visual acuity (BCDVA) examined using a Snellen chart (automatic chart projector; TCP-4042; Tomey Co; Nagoya, Japan). A slit lamp (Slit-lamp, TSL-800H, Tomey Corp., Japan) was used to evaluate the anterior and posterior segments in cooperative children; however, examination under anesthesia was performed for younger children. Intraocular pressure was measured using the Goldmann applanation tonometer (AT900, Haag-Streit, Koeniz, Switzerland) or Tono-Pen XL (Medtronic Solan, Jacksonville, FL, USA). B-scan ultrasonography (EZ-Scan, A/B 5500 plus, Sonomed-USA) was used to evaluate the posterior segment in patients with diffuse severe corneal opacity. Five surgeons performed all surgeries under general anesthesia. Donor corneas were imported from the Jordan Eye Bank, where they had been screened for infectious agents and endothelial quality. ## Branch report on endothelial keratoplasty advantages and challenges

### Which pediatric indications make endothelial keratoplasty most appropriate?

In pediatric patients, endothelial keratoplasty (EK) is most appropriate when the primary corneal problem is **endothelial dysfunction with minimal stromal involvement**. The strongest pediatric EK evidence in the search result set reports that **congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED)** was the most reported indication in pediatric DSAEK, with **108 eyes** included in the systematic review/individual participant data meta-analysis [N1-F1]. That same source also notes that EK is increasingly considered the first intervention in pediatrics with **isolated corneal endothelial dysfunction** [N1-F1]. Other pediatric EK indications included **Descemet’s membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK)** in rare cases, such as **PPCD** and **Kearns-Sayre syndrome** [N1-F1].

The pediatric-specific context is important because young patients often have **robust corneal tissue** and may benefit from preserving more native stroma than full-thickness PKP [N4-R1]. This supports EK as a preferred option for diseases primarily involving the **endothelium or Descemet’s membrane**, rather than widespread stromal disease.

### How the procedure compares with penetrating keratoplasty in terms of wound healing and complication risk

EK is generally associated with **faster visual recovery**, **less astigmatism**, and **elimination of suture and wound-related complications** compared with penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) [N3-R4]. It also has **lower intraoperative risk** and is said to improve wound integrity [N3-R1]. In the pediatric EK evidence, the most reported complication was **graft dislocation** in 26 eyes, while other complication rates were described as low [N1-F1]. Endothelial cell loss was reported from **8.3 to 63.7%** after pediatric EK, with follow-up ranging from 3 months to 8.3 years [N1-F1].

In contrast, PKP is associated with a higher risk of **early graft edema** and **suture-related complications** [N2-R4]. The broader corneal-transplant context notes that pediatric patients undergoing corneal transplants are at high risk for **graft infection, failure, rejection, dehiscence, and amblyopia** due to young age and robust corneal architecture [N4-R1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that EK has a more favorable **early wound-healing profile** and lower early complication burden than PKP, though the pediatric EK evidence does identify specific risks such as graft dislocation and endothelial cell loss [N1-F1; N3-R4].

### How pediatric-specific factors like graft size and donor tissue quality affect outcomes

Pediatric-specific factors are critical to EK outcomes. The pediatric EK review notes that some **anatomical and physiological pediatric characteristics** require modifications to the standard procedure [N1-F1]. This implies that **graft size**, **recipient corneal dimensions**, and **donor tissue quality** are important in planning and execution. The evidence also highlights **endothelial cell loss** as a function of the procedure and follow-up duration, which suggests that donor tissue quality and postoperative management are key determinants of long-term endothelial stability [N1-F1].

The broader pediatric transplant context adds that young age, robust corneal structure, and growth-related challenges make graft sizing and donor matching more sensitive in children [N4-R1]. Although the provided evidence does not quantify graft size effects in pediatric EK directly, it does emphasize that **pediatric-specific modifications** are needed to account for size-related challenges [N1-F1]. For donor tissue quality, the evidence indirectly supports its importance through the emphasis on endothelial cell loss and the need for **endothelial quality screening** in PKP donor corneas [N2-F2]. Thus, in pediatric EK, **smaller grafts, tight fit, and high-quality endothelial tissue** are likely to improve outcomes, while mismatched or compromised donor tissue can worsen endothelial stability [N1-F1; N4-R1].

## Branch report on penetrating keratoplasty advantages and challenges

### Which pediatric indications make penetrating keratoplasty more appropriate?

Penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) remains more appropriate in pediatric patients when the corneal pathology involves **widespread disease** or when **lamellar techniques are not suitable**. The pediatric PKP evidence notes that PKP is the gold standard for improving visual acuity, retaining structural integrity, and avoiding deprivation amblyopia [N2-F2]. It is also described as the preferred approach when the indication is **congenital or acquired non-traumatic corneal pathologies** [N2-F2]. In the Jordan retrospective study, the most frequent indication was **advanced keratoconus**, and **acquired non-traumatic corneal pathologies** accounted for **65.8%** of pediatric PKP indications [N2-F2]. The broader pediatric transplant context adds that PKP is also used for **congenital corneal opacities** and that it may be necessary when lamellar keratoplasty is not feasible [N4-R1].

In other words, PKP is more appropriate when the disease burden is **more extensive** or when the patient has **structural instability** requiring full-thickness replacement, or when **lamellar techniques are not indicated**. It is also the main option when **deprivation amblyopia prevention** is a priority [N2-F2].

### How the procedure compares with endothelial keratoplasty in terms of technical difficulty and learning curve

PKP is generally more technically demanding than EK, especially in pediatric patients. The pediatric PKP evidence states that PKP can be technically more challenging than adult keratoplasty because of **thinner corneas, lower scleral rigidity, anatomically smaller eyes, and other intraoperative obstacles** [N2-R3]. It also notes that pediatric PKP has **difficult preoperative evaluation, multiple intraoperative obstacles, and challenges in post-operative follow-up and management** [N2-R1; N2-F2]. These factors imply a steeper learning curve and higher technical demands.

In contrast, EK is described as having **lower intraoperative risk**, **faster visual recovery**, and elimination of suture and wound-related complications [N3-R4]. The broader corneal-transplant context also supports the idea that EK is less technically burdensome in terms of wound handling and early postoperative stability [N4-R1]. Overall, PKP has a higher technical difficulty and learning curve in pediatric patients, while EK is more streamlined and less dependent on suture management [N2-R1; N2-R3; N3-R4].

### How pediatric-specific factors like rejection and postoperative astigmatism affect outcomes

Pediatric-specific factors significantly affect PKP outcomes. The corneal-transplant context notes that pediatric patients are at high risk for **graft infection, failure, rejection, dehiscence, and amblyopia** [N4-R1]. It also states that **corneal neovascularization** may suggest lower graft survival and that **glaucoma** is an important risk factor [N4-R4]. In the pediatric PKP evidence, the most frequent indication was **advanced keratoconus**, and the study reports a **1-year graft survival rate of 80.54%** [N2-F2].

Rejection and postoperative astigmatism are important in PKP outcomes. While the provided evidence does not quantify rejection rates specifically in pediatric PKP, the broader corneal-transplant context identifies **immunologic allograft rejection** as the most common cause of graft failure [N4-R2]. The pediatric PKP evidence also highlights that **preoperative and postoperative visual acuity** can change significantly, with some patients showing improved, worsened, or unchanged visual acuity [N2-F2]. This suggests that **postoperative astigmatism and refractive instability** may affect visual outcomes, even if the provided evidence does not explicitly separate them from rejection.

In summary, pediatric PKP is more susceptible to rejection, infection, dehiscence, and glaucoma-related complications, while postoperative astigmatism and refractive changes are likely to affect visual recovery [N2-F2; N4-R1; N4-R2; N4-R4].

## Branch report on comparative short-term vs long-term outcomes and evidence quality

### Which procedure has better short-term visual recovery and fewer early complications

The evidence supports **EK** as having better short-term visual recovery than PKP. EK is described as associated with **faster visual recovery**, **less astigmatism**, and **elimination of suture and wound-related complications** compared with PKP [N3-R4]. The pediatric EK evidence also notes that graft dislocation was the most reported complication, but the overall complication rate was described as low [N1-F1]. In contrast, PKP is associated with **early graft edema** in **50.8%** of PKP patients in one direct comparison, which was significantly higher than in DALK patients [N2-R4].

For pediatric patients, the evidence suggests that EK is particularly attractive for early visual recovery because it avoids suture-related problems and has a faster recovery profile [N3-R1; N3-R4]. PKP, on the other hand, carries more early wound and suture-related risks [N2-R4; N2-R1].

### Which procedure has better long-term graft survival and fewer late complications

The long-term evidence favors **EK** for better long-term graft survival, while **PKP** may have better short-term survival. The Dutch registry study found that **five-year survival was comparable for EK and PK** overall, but **long-term graft survival was better after EK** and **short-term survival was better after PK** [N5-F3; N5-R2]. The same source also states that EK graft survival improved significantly over time while remaining stable, which suggests that EK has durable long-term benefits [N5-F3].

The pediatric corneal-transplant context also supports the idea that pediatric graft failure is common and that rejection and other late complications remain important risks [N4-R2; N4-R3]. In pediatric PKP, the 1-year graft survival rate was **80.54%**, but the evidence notes that longer follow-up is needed to assess long-term survival [N2-F2]. In the broader pediatric transplant context, the most common cause of graft failure is **immunologic allograft rejection**, and **unknown causes** account for a substantial fraction of failures [N4-R2; N4-R3].

Thus, EK appears to have better long-term graft survival and fewer late complications, while PKP may have a better early survival profile [N5-F3; N5-R2; N2-F2].

### How evidence quality differs for pediatric versus adult populations

The evidence quality difference is clear: the pediatric evidence is **less abundant and more limited** than adult evidence. The pediatric EK evidence includes a systematic review/individual participant data meta-analysis of **35 articles** and **154 eyes**, which is substantial for a pediatric topic but still limited in scale compared with adult cohorts [N1-F1]. The pediatric PKP evidence includes a **retrospective observational study** of **149 cases** in Jordan, which is a large pediatric series but still retrospective and limited by single-center bias [N2-F2].

In contrast, the adult EK vs PKP evidence in the search result set includes a **Dutch registry study** and other comparative studies with more mature methodologies [N5-F3; N5-R1; N5-R2]. The Dutch registry is prospective and multicenter, which strengthens its evidence quality relative to pediatric studies [N5-F3]. The broader pediatric transplant context also notes that pediatric outcomes are affected by **growth, amblyopia, and corneal size**, which are not always fully captured in adult studies [N4-R1; N4-R3; N4-R4].

Overall, the pediatric evidence is **lower quality overall**, with more reliance on retrospective studies, smaller sample sizes, and less long-term follow-up than adult evidence [N2-F2; N1-F1; N5-F3].

### Whether pediatric age groups show distinct outcome patterns

Yes, pediatric age groups appear to show distinct outcome patterns. The pediatric PKP evidence reports a mean age of **11.44 ± 4.97 years** at the time of surgery and notes that **age < 18 years** defines pediatric PKP [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that PKP is rarely performed in children and has a **high rate of graft failure and poor visual outcomes** compared with adult keratoplasty [N2-F2]. The broader pediatric transplant context adds that **young age** and **robust corneal architecture** increase the risk of graft infection, failure, rejection, dehiscence, and amblyopia [N4-R1].

In pediatric EK, the evidence is even more age-specific because the review explicitly focuses on **pediatric EK** and reports that the most reported indication was CHED, which is typically a congenital or childhood disease [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that **pediatric-specific modifications** are needed because of anatomical and physiological differences [N1-F1]. This indicates that outcomes differ by age group, with younger children likely facing more challenges related to **growth, amblyopia, and donor tissue matching** than older children.

In summary, the evidence suggests that pediatric patients have distinct outcome patterns, including higher failure risk, more amblyopia risk, and more dependence on graft size and donor quality, compared with adults [N2-F2; N4-R1; N4-R3; N4-R4].

## Branch report on pediatric-specific graft failure and complication drivers

### The most common pediatric graft failure and rejection mechanisms

The most common pediatric graft failure mechanism is **immunologic allograft rejection**, as the corneal-transplant context explicitly states that despite being an "immunologically privileged" site, the most common cause of graft failure is **irreversible, immunologic allograft rejection** [N4-R2]. The pediatric transplant context also notes that graft failure may be due to **unknown causes**, with **44%** of failures in one study attributed to unknown causes [N4-R3]. This means rejection is the primary failure mechanism, but pediatric graft failure is also influenced by other non-immunologic factors.

### How amblyopia, infection, dehiscence, and glaucoma affect outcomes

Pediatric corneal transplants are particularly vulnerable to multiple late complications. The pediatric transplant context reports that children are at high risk for **graft infection, failure, rejection, dehiscence, and amblyopia** due to young age and robust corneal architecture [N4-R1]. It also states that **corneal neovascularization** may suggest lower graft survival and that **glaucoma** is an important risk factor [N4-R4]. 

Amblyopia is especially important in pediatric transplants because the goal is to avoid **deprivation amblyopia** [N2-F2]. The broader evidence also notes that **visual acuity may worsen, improve, or remain unchanged postoperatively**, which is relevant for amblyopia prevention and treatment [N2-F2]. Infection, dehiscence, and glaucoma therefore compound the risk of poor visual and anatomical outcomes in children.

### How pediatric-specific factors like donor tissue quality and corneal size influence risk

Donor tissue quality and corneal size are central to pediatric transplant outcomes. The pediatric EK evidence notes that some **anatomical and physiological pediatric characteristics** require modifications to the standard procedure [N1-F1], which implies that **smaller grafts and tighter fit** are important. The evidence also highlights **endothelial cell loss**, which is likely influenced by donor tissue quality and postoperative handling [N1-F1]. In PKP, donor tissue quality is explicitly mentioned in the Jordan PKP study, which reports that donor corneas were imported and screened for infectious agents and endothelial quality [N2-F2].

Corneal size matters because pediatric patients often have **smaller eyes, thinner corneas, and lower scleral rigidity**, making graft sizing and fit more sensitive [N2-R3; N4-R1]. These pediatric-specific factors increase the risk of dehiscence and graft dislocation [N4-R1; N1-F1]. In short, high-quality donor tissue and well-matched graft size are protective factors, while poor tissue quality or mismatched graft dimensions increase rejection, dislocation, and graft failure risk [N1-F1; N2-F2; N4-R1].

### How early graft survival relates to long-term graft survival

Early graft survival is closely related to long-term graft survival, but the evidence suggests that this relationship is not perfect. The pediatric transplant context reports that **14% of pediatric grafts failed**, with **65% failing within 2 years post-graft** [N4-R3]. This indicates that early failure is a strong predictor of long-term failure. In PKP, the 1-year graft survival rate was **80.54%** in one pediatric study, but longer follow-up is needed to confirm long-term survival [N2-F2].

The broader evidence also indicates that **early complications** such as infection, dehiscence, and rejection can lead to long-term graft loss [N4-R2; N4-R3]. In EK, graft dislocation was the most reported complication, and endothelial cell loss was reported across a wide range of follow-up periods [N1-F1]. This suggests that even if early graft survival is good, later complications can still threaten long-term survival.

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that **early graft survival is a strong prognostic indicator of long-term graft survival in pediatric patients**, but it is not the only determinant [N4-R3; N2-F2; N1-F1].

# Integrated final answer: endothelial keratoplasty versus penetrating keratoplasty in pediatric patients

## Overall comparison framework

In pediatric corneal transplantation, **endothelial keratoplasty (EK)** and **penetrating keratoplasty (PKP)** are chosen based on disease type, corneal involvement, and surgical goals. The evidence indicates that EK is increasingly considered the first intervention for pediatric patients with **isolated corneal endothelial dysfunction** and minimal stromal involvement [N1-F1], whereas PKP remains more appropriate when the disease burden is more extensive or when lamellar techniques are not feasible [N2-F2]. Across both procedures, pediatric-specific factors such as **graft size, donor tissue quality, rejection, amblyopia risk, and growth-related challenges** strongly influence outcomes [N4-R1; N4-R2; N4-R4].

## Which procedure is more appropriate for which pediatric indications?

### Endothelial keratoplasty: best for endothelial disease with minimal stromal involvement

EK is most appropriate when the primary problem is **endothelial dysfunction**. In pediatric EK evidence, **congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED)** was the most reported indication, with **108 eyes** included in the systematic review [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that EK is increasingly considered the first intervention in pediatrics with **isolated corneal endothelial dysfunction** [N1-F1]. This makes EK especially suitable for congenital or inherited endothelial disorders where the stroma is minimally affected [N1-F1; N4-R1].

EK is also used for rare pediatric indications such as **Descemet’s membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK)** in cases of **PPCD** and **Kearns-Sayre syndrome** [N1-F1]. In these settings, preserving more native stroma is important because young patients often have **robust corneal tissue** [N4-R1].

### Penetrating keratoplasty: more appropriate for widespread disease or when lamellar techniques are not indicated

PKP remains more appropriate when the pathology is more extensive or when **lamellar keratoplasty is not feasible**. PKP is described as the gold standard for improving visual acuity, retaining structural integrity, and avoiding deprivation amblyopia [N2-F2]. In the Jordan pediatric PKP study, the most frequent indication was **advanced keratoconus**, and **acquired non-traumatic corneal pathologies** accounted for **65.8%** of pediatric PKP indications [N2-F2]. It is also used for **congenital corneal opacities** [N4-R1].

In other words, PKP is more appropriate when the disease burden is **widespread**, when **structural instability** requires full-thickness replacement, or when **deprivation amblyopia prevention** is a priority [N2-F2; N4-R1].

## How the procedures compare in terms of wound healing and complication risk

### EK: faster visual recovery and lower early complication burden

EK is generally associated with **faster visual recovery**, **less astigmatism**, and **elimination of suture and wound-related complications** compared with PKP [N3-R4]. It also has **lower intraoperative risk** and is said to improve wound integrity [N3-R1]. In the pediatric EK evidence, the most reported complication was **graft dislocation** in **26 eyes**, while other complication rates were described as low [N1-F1]. Endothelial cell loss was reported from **8.3 to 63.7%** after pediatric EK [N1-F1].

### PKP: higher early wound and suture-related risks

PKP is associated with a higher risk of **early graft edema** and **suture-related complications** [N2-R4]. The broader pediatric transplant context notes that children undergoing corneal transplants are at high risk for **graft infection, failure, rejection, dehiscence, and amblyopia** due to young age and robust corneal architecture [N4-R1]. PKP also carries a higher technical burden in pediatric patients because of **thinner corneas, lower scleral rigidity, anatomically smaller eyes, and other intraoperative obstacles** [N2-R3; N2-R1]. These factors contribute to a **steeper learning curve** and higher technical difficulty [N2-R3; N2-R1].

## How pediatric-specific factors affect outcomes

### Graft size and donor tissue quality

Pediatric-specific factors are central to both EK and PKP outcomes. The pediatric EK evidence notes that some **anatomical and physiological pediatric characteristics** require modifications to the standard procedure [N1-F1]. This implies that **graft size, recipient corneal dimensions, and donor tissue quality** are important in planning and execution. The evidence also highlights **endothelial cell loss** as a function of the procedure and follow-up duration, suggesting that **high-quality donor tissue** and careful graft matching are critical for long-term stability [N1-F1; N4-R1].

In PKP, donor tissue quality is explicitly mentioned in the Jordan PKP study, which reports that donor corneas were imported and screened for infectious agents and endothelial quality [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that **donor tissue quality** is a major determinant of outcome, especially in pediatric patients where graft fit and endothelial stability are more sensitive.

### Growth-related considerations

Pediatric patients also face growth-related challenges. The broader pediatric transplant context notes that **young age** and **robust corneal architecture** increase the risk of graft infection, failure, rejection, dehiscence, and amblyopia [N4-R1]. It also emphasizes that **growth** affects corneal size and structural integrity, which in turn influences graft sizing and long-term stability [N4-R1].

## Comparative short-term vs long-term outcomes

### Short-term visual recovery and early complications

The evidence favors **EK** for better short-term visual recovery and fewer early complications. EK is described as associated with **faster visual recovery**, **less astigmatism**, and elimination of suture and wound-related complications compared with PKP [N3-R4]. In pediatric EK evidence, the most reported complication was **graft dislocation**, but the overall complication rate was described as low [N1-F1]. In contrast, PKP is associated with **early graft edema** in **50.8%** of PKP patients, significantly more than in DALK patients [N2-R4].

### Long-term graft survival and late complications

The long-term evidence favors **EK** for better long-term graft survival, while **PKP** may have better short-term survival. The Dutch registry study found that **five-year survival was comparable for EK and PK** overall, but **long-term graft survival was better after EK** and **short-term survival was better after PK** [N5-F3; N5-R2]. The same source also states that EK graft survival improved significantly over time while remaining stable, which suggests durable long-term benefits [N5-F3].

For pediatric PKP, the evidence indicates a **1-year graft survival rate of 80.54%** in one study, but longer follow-up is needed to assess long-term survival [N2-F2]. The broader pediatric transplant context also supports the idea that **immunologic allograft rejection** is the most common cause of graft failure, and that **unknown causes** account for a substantial fraction of failures [N4-R2; N4-R3].

## Evidence quality differences

The evidence quality is **lower for pediatric populations** than for adults.
